title: Preparing for surgery: assessment, fasting and diabetes
blurb: Prepare adults for surgery safely: modern fasting times, carbohydrate drinks, prehabilitation, preoperative checks, and the JBDS rules for people with diabetes.
question: Mrs Hartley, 58, is first on the afternoon list at 14:00. A colleague tells her she cannot drink anything after midnight. What clear-fluid advice reflects current guidance?

teach.h: Get people to theatre in the best shape
teach.body: Preoperative preparation aims to make surgery as safe as possible and recovery as quick as possible. It covers risk assessment and shared decisions, optimising health (prehabilitation), safe fasting, the right medicines on the day, and specific plans for conditions such as diabetes. Plain English: avoid long, unnecessary starvation, fix what can be fixed before the operation, and make sure everyone knows the plan.

items.label: Last solid food (8 h+ after a large fatty meal)
Restart fluids and diet as soon as feasible

teach.caption: NICE NG180 rec 1.4.1: clear fluids until 2 hours before the operation. The 2026 international consensus (FAST26) agrees: food at least 6 hours, clear liquids until 2 hours.

teach.h: What counts as a clear fluid? (NG180 1.4.1)
teach.caption: NICE adds that drinking clear fluids before surgery can reduce headaches, nausea and vomiting afterwards. FAST26 allows a little milk; NICE does not, so follow local policy.

teach.text: 'Nil by mouth from midnight' is outdated for most adults. Clear fluids are allowed until 2 hours before anaesthesia and solids until 6 hours. Long fasting causes dehydration, headache, nausea and, in diabetes, hypoglycaemia. Also: NBM time is counted to anaesthesia, not to the time on the list.

items: Use a validated risk stratification tool alongside clinical assessment, and discuss risks and options.
Discuss lifestyle changes: stopping smoking and reducing alcohol.
Treat iron-deficiency anaemia before surgery (NICE blood transfusion guidance).
Offer an enhanced recovery programme for elective major or complex surgery.
Consider carbohydrate drinks before major or complex abdominal surgery.

head: Medicine
Day before
Morning list
teach.caption: *If eGFR above 60 and no contrast. With contrast and eGFR below 60, omit metformin on the day and for 48 hours after. People on SGLT-2 inhibitors need daily ketone checks in hospital.

teach.body: HbA1c should be checked within 3 months before surgery; refer for diabetes support if it is above 69 mmol/mol (8.5%). People with diabetes should be first on the list to minimise fasting. Aim for capillary glucose 6–10 mmol/L (up to 12 acceptable). Use a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII) when more than one meal will be missed; continue long-acting basal insulin at 80% of the usual dose.

items.label: mmol/mol HbA1c: above this, optimise first
most recent HbA1c within this time

teach.body: Mr Diallo, 62, has type 2 diabetes on metformin, gliclazide and dapagliflozin, eGFR 75, and is having a morning laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His HbA1c last month was 58. The preassessment nurse gives written advice: omit dapagliflozin the day before and on the day; omit gliclazide that morning; take metformin as normal; eat until 6 hours and drink clear fluids until 2 hours before anaesthesia. She books him first on the list.

items: Clear fluids until 2 hours, food until 6 hours before anaesthesia; no routine NBM from midnight.
Clear fluids: water, pulp-free juice, tea or coffee without milk, ice lollies.
Consider carbohydrate drinks before major abdominal surgery; offer enhanced recovery.
Diabetes: HbA1c within 3 months, optimise if above 69; first on the list; glucose 6–10.
SGLT-2 inhibitor: omit day before and day of surgery; sulfonylurea: omit on the morning.

summary: You can now give safe, current fasting advice and support preoperative optimisation and enhanced recovery. You can also prepare a person with diabetes for surgery, from HbA1c and list order to which medicines to omit and the perioperative glucose target.

A.q: Mrs Hartley, 58, is having elective surgery under general anaesthesia at 14:00. Until what time may she drink clear fluids, according to NICE NG180?
A.why: NICE NG180 rec 1.4.1: people having surgery may drink clear fluids until 2 hours before their operation. For 14:00 that is 12:00.

whyNot.0: Midnight fasting is outdated and causes unnecessary dehydration.
whyNot.1: 08:00 is 6 hours before: the limit for solid food, not clear fluids.
whyNot.3: 06:00 is 8 hours before, far longer than needed for clear fluids.

A.q: Which drink counts as a clear fluid under NICE NG180 on the morning of surgery?
A.why: NICE NG180 rec 1.4.1: clear fluids are water, fruit juice without pulp, coffee or tea without milk, and ice lollies.

whyNot.0: Juice with pulp is not a clear fluid.
whyNot.1: Protein shakes are not clear fluids.
whyNot.2: NICE defines tea and coffee as clear when taken without milk.

A.q: Mr Diallo takes dapagliflozin and is having surgery on Thursday. When should the SGLT-2 inhibitor be omitted?
A.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: omit SGLT-2 inhibitors the day before surgery and on the day of surgery, with daily ketone checks in hospital.

whyNot.0: Omitting on the day alone does not follow JBDS; the day before is omitted too.
whyNot.1: JBDS sets the day before and the day of surgery, not a week.
whyNot.3: SGLT-2 inhibitors are withheld because of the risk of DKA.

B.q: Mrs Grant, 66, with type 2 diabetes is referred for a hip replacement. Her HbA1c is 76 mmol/mol. What does JBDS advise?
options: Optimise and refer for diabetes support first
Proceed; HbA1c does not affect surgery
Start insulin on the day of surgery
B.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: aim to optimise glycaemic control, aiming for HbA1c below 69 mmol/mol (8.5%) before surgery, and refer for diabetes specialist support if above 69.

whyNot.1: Suboptimal control raises perioperative risk; JBDS says optimise first.
whyNot.2: JBDS advises optimising control and referring for specialist support; it does not cancel surgery.
whyNot.3: Starting insulin on the day is not optimisation and risks hypoglycaemia.

B.q: Mr Walsh takes gliclazide twice daily and is on a morning list. What should happen to his gliclazide on the morning of surgery?
options: Take it with a carbohydrate drink
B.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: omit sulfonylureas on the morning of surgery for a morning list (take the evening dose if eating).

whyNot.0: A sulfonylurea while fasting risks hypoglycaemia.
whyNot.1: A half dose still risks hypoglycaemia while fasting.
whyNot.3: A carbohydrate drink does not make the sulfonylurea dose safe; it is omitted.

B.q: During the perioperative period, what capillary glucose range does JBDS recommend for people with diabetes?
B.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: aim to keep capillary glucose 6–10 mmol/L (up to 12 mmol/L is acceptable).

whyNot.0: 4–7 is the NG17 pre-meal target for type 1 diabetes.
whyNot.2: 4–11 is the NG128 acute stroke range.

C.q: Ms Obi, 44, with type 1 diabetes, is having major bowel surgery and will miss several meals. Which insulin plan matches JBDS?
options: Stop all insulin until eating again
Usual rapid-acting insulin with each missed meal
C.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: a VRIII is preferred when more than one meal will be missed, and long-acting insulin analogues are continued at 80% of the usual dose.

whyNot.1: Stopping all insulin in type 1 diabetes causes DKA.
whyNot.2: Mealtime insulin without meals causes hypoglycaemia.
whyNot.3: A subcutaneous sliding scale is not the JBDS approach for prolonged fasting.

C.q: Mr Diallo, 62, has type 2 diabetes on metformin twice daily with eGFR 75. His operation does not involve contrast. What should he do with his metformin?
options: Switch to insulin for the day
C.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: if eGFR is above 60 and no contrast is used, once- or twice-daily metformin is taken as normal.

whyNot.0: Omitting for 48 hours applies after contrast when eGFR is below 60.
whyNot.2: Metformin is taken as normal the day before.
whyNot.3: No switch to insulin is needed for a short fast.

C.q: Mrs Field, 70, is having a major abdominal operation on an enhanced recovery pathway. She is not diabetic. Which preoperative intervention should be considered under NICE NG180?
options: Bed rest the day before surgery
C.why: NICE NG180 rec 1.4.2: consider carbohydrate drinks before surgery for people having major or complex abdominal surgery.

whyNot.0: Clear fluids are allowed until 2 hours before; midnight fasting is outdated.
whyNot.2: Routine bowel preparation is not an NG180 preoperative recommendation.
whyNot.3: Bed rest undermines prehabilitation and early mobilising.

reteach.title: Six, two, and the diabetes checklist
reteach.question: If you could remember only two numbers for fasting and one checklist for diabetes, what would they be?

blocks.body: Six hours: last food. Two hours: last clear drink (water, pulp-free juice, black tea or coffee). Diabetes checklist: HbA1c within 3 months (optimise if above 69), first on the list, SGLT-2 inhibitor off the day before and the day of surgery, sulfonylurea off the morning of surgery, metformin usually as normal, VRIII if more than one meal missed, glucose 6–10.

blocks.text: Black coffee is a clear fluid under NICE; a latte is not.

explain.body: Clear fluids until 2 hours before; solids at least 6 hours (8+ after a large fatty meal). Restart fluids and diet as soon as feasible after anaesthesia.

test.q: A man's operation is at 10:00. What is the latest he should eat a light breakfast?
test.why: The 2026 international fasting consensus (FAST26): solid food at least 6 hours before anaesthesia. 10:00 minus 6 hours is 04:00.

explain.body: Validated risk tool and shared decisions; stop smoking and reduce alcohol; treat iron-deficiency anaemia; enhanced recovery for elective major surgery; carbohydrate drinks before major abdominal surgery.

test.q: A woman due for major surgery in 6 weeks has iron-deficiency anaemia. What does NICE NG180 advise?
options: Transfuse on the day of surgery
Leave it untreated if Hb is above 80
test.why: NICE NG180 rec 1.3.4: for people with iron-deficiency anaemia having surgery, follow NICE blood transfusion guidance on IV and oral iron, treating it before surgery.

whyNot.0: Transfusion is not the first-line approach to iron deficiency before planned surgery.
whyNot.2: There is no Hb cut-off for leaving iron deficiency untreated.
whyNot.3: A year's delay is not needed; iron treatment works in weeks.

explain.body: HbA1c within the last 3 months (NG45); refer for optimisation if above 69 mmol/mol. People with diabetes go first on the list to minimise fasting.

test.q: A man with diabetes is booked for elective surgery. His last HbA1c was 5 months ago. What does NICE NG45 advise?
test.why: NICE NG45 rec 1.6.2: offer HbA1c testing to people with diabetes having surgery if they have not been tested in the last 3 months.

whyNot.0: A result over 3 months old is out of date for this purpose.
whyNot.1: The result is needed beforehand to plan optimisation.
whyNot.2: HbA1c is indicated in people with diabetes.

explain.body: SGLT-2 inhibitors: omit day before and day of surgery. Sulfonylureas: omit on the morning. Metformin: as normal if eGFR above 60 and no contrast. VRIII if more than one meal missed; glucose 6–10 (up to 12).

test.q: When is a VRIII the preferred method of managing glucose around surgery, according to JBDS?
options: When more than one meal is missed
test.why: JBDS 03/CPOC 2022: a VRIII is preferred for people with diabetes having surgery with a fasting period of more than one missed meal (among other indications).

whyNot.0: A short fast (no more than one missed meal) can usually be managed with medication adjustment.
whyNot.2: Many people with short fasts do not need a VRIII.
whyNot.3: 6–10 is the target range, not an indication for a VRIII.
